St. Demetrius of Thessalonica

Saints

St. Demetrius of Thessalonica

Demetrios · Dēmḗtrios

Period
Early Church period; exact chronology not established here
Region
Balkans
Titles / vocation
Martyr · Military saint
Commemoration
October 26

Introduction

St. Demetrius, also rendered Demetrios, is remembered as a martyr of Thessalonica and as the Myrrh-gusher. The source describes his public position, Christian confession, and suffering during imperial persecution. It also recounts his later veneration and connections with Slavic Christian history. This profile identifies that ecclesiastical narrative and does not confuse him with other saints bearing the same name.

Background

The Orthodox life places St. Demetrius in Thessalonica, raised by Christian parents and appointed proconsul. He openly teaches Christ after his father’s death.

[1] Ecclesiastical saint’s life · Published life, body paragraph 1; opening: The Great Martyr Demetrios (Dēmḗtrios) the Myrrh-gusher of Thessaloniki was…

Baring-Gould’s 1898 retelling below follows a different Passion recension. It omits Nestor’s visit for a blessing and places Demetrius’s confinement in the public baths; these differences remain attributed to their sources.

[2] Historical hagiographic retelling · pp.165–167; source introduction and comparison of Passion recensions

Life and notable events

Maximianus Galerius was at Thessalonica about the year 306, where he amused his leisure with gladiatorial fights in the amphitheatre. He had a favourite gladiator, named Lyæus, a man large of body, powerful and agile; he had been the death of so many men, that scarce any could be found who would meet him in the arena. One day, Maximian went to the amphitheatre accompanied by Lyæus, when he was met on the road by his officers, conveying Demetrius, a Christian, whom they had apprehended, to prison. Maximian halted, and ordered him to be thrust into a room in the public baths till he returned from the sports, when he would examine him himself. Then he strode on and took his accustomed place in the circus. Lyæus stood forth in the arena, and defied all men to contend with him. No one accepted the challenge. Then Maximian offered large rewards to the man who would fight with Lyæus. Instantly a young man named Nestor jumped into the middle of the lists, and offered to fight the practised gladiator. Maximian hesitated, then called the youth up to him and said, “Hark ye, I know that you have challenged Lyæus because you are needy; and you think, if you kill him, you will gain great rewards; and if you die—well, there is an end to poverty and misery. But, young man, I have pity on your youth, and I will give you a present because of your pluck in defying this champion of mine.” “Sire,” answered Nestor, “I have not challenged him for reward, but for the honour of fighting so redoubted a gladiator.”

[2] Historical hagiographic retelling · pp.165–166; arena, arrest, and Nestor’s challenge

Death and martyrdom

So they met, and Lyæus was prostrated at one blow and killed. Maximian was angry at having lost his favourite fighting-man. He rose from his seat, and left the amphitheatre without rewarding Nestor. He was in this mood, when the officers stood before him on his way home and asked what was to be done with Demetrius.

“Run him through with your spears,” said the angry tyrant. And Demetrius, unheard, was thus privately despatched in a room of the baths.

[2] Historical hagiographic retelling · p.166; imperial anger and death by spears

The OCA life dates his lancing to October 26, 306, and records Lupus collecting his garment and ring, then Christians recovering his body.

[1] Ecclesiastical saint’s life · Published life: prison death, Lupus, and burial

Writings and legacy

When persecution ceased, Leontius, Christian prefect of Illyria, purged the baths, and erected over the scene of the martyrdom and the body of the martyr, a Christian church, which he also richly endowed, in honour of the martyr Demetrius. The later historians of the passion, to connect the incidents and exalt the saint, make Nestor ask his blessing before he engages with Lyæus, but there is no hint of this in the earliest Acts.

[2] Historical hagiographic retelling · pp.166–167; Leontius’s church and comparison of narratives

His shrine’s myrrh gives him the title Myrrh-gusher.

[1] Ecclesiastical saint’s life · Published life: relics and myrrh

Image details

Saint Demetrius of Protat.JPG

Saint Demetrios of Thessalonica , fresco by Manuel Panselinos in the Protaton Church . Saint Demetrios came from a wealthy family and because he was athletic in appearance and heroic in spirit, he became a high-ranking officer in the Roman army at a very young age. This is why he is depicted in Byzantine icons in military dress, either standing or riding a horse. Throughout his life, he considered himself a soldier of Christ first, and a military soldier second.
